🐛 Bug
When a module is composed of nested modules and a the model registers a state_dict hook for sharded tensors, the time to retrieve the state_dict increases exponentially with the depth of nesting.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
from torch import nn
from torch.nn.modules.container import ModuleDict
from torch.distributed._sharded_tensor import state_dict_hook


class LitAutoEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, depth):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_dict = depth

        def recursive_build_encoder(stop_num, current_num):
            if stop_num == current_num:
                return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(current_num + 1, current_num + 1))
            else:
                module_dict = ModuleDict()
                module_dict[str(current_num)] = recursive_build_encoder(stop_num, current_num + 1)
                return module_dict

        self.encoder = recursive_build_encoder(depth, 0)

        # register state dict hook
        self._register_state_dict_hook(state_dict_hook)


# this does not terminate in a reasonable time!
enc = LitAutoEncoder(depth=100)
enc.state_dict()
This Python script will not terminate within a reasonable time. For very small numbers of depth it is not noticeable.

Expected behavior
The state dict retrieval time should be linear in the number of submodules.
Possible fix
I believe the implementation of this function is inefficient as it redundantly recurses:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/_sharded_tensor/__init__.py
    
    
        Lines 375 to 382
      in
      c41d829
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def _recurse_update_dict(module, destination, prefix): 
        

        
          
               for attr_name, attr in module.__dict__.items(): 
        

        
          
                   if isinstance(attr, ShardedTensor): 
        

        
          
                       destination[prefix + attr_name] = attr 
        

        
          
            
        

        
          
               for submodule_name, submodule in module.named_modules(): 
        

        
          
                   if submodule_name != '': 
        

        
          
                       _recurse_update_dict(submodule, destination, prefix + submodule_name + '.') 
        
    
  


From what I can tell, the recursion is not necessary, because module.named_modules() ALREADY returns all the nested submodules in a generator. I would instead propose this:
def _recurse_update_dict(module, destination, prefix):
    for submodule_name, submodule in module.named_modules():
        for attr_name, attr in module.__dict__.items():
            if isinstance(attr, ShardedTensor):
                destination[prefix + submodule_name + "." + attr_name] = attr

🐛 Bug

According to the documentation:

Every Sampler subclass has to provide an __iter__() method, providing a way to iterate over indices of dataset elements, and a __len__() method that returns the length of the returned iterators.

However, the Sampler base class does not include __len__ as an @abstractmethod. This causes mypy to not identify identify samplers as sized objects.
To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior: call `mypy` on the following snippet
from abc import abstractmethod
from collections.abc import Sized
from typing import Generic, Iterator, Optional, TypeVar
from torch.utils.data import Sampler, SequentialSampler

T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)


class MySampler(Generic[T_co]):
    r"""Base class for all Samplers.

    Every Sampler subclass has to provide an :meth:`__iter__` method, providing a
    way to iterate over indices of dataset elements, and a :meth:`__len__` method
    that returns the length of the returned iterators.

    .. note:: The :meth:`__len__` method isn't strictly required by
              :class:`~torch.utils.data.DataLoader`, but is expected in any
              calculation involving the length of a :class:`~torch.utils.data.DataLoader`.
    """

    @abstractmethod
    def __init__(self, data_source: Optional[Sized]) -> None:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[T_co]:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def __len__(self) -> int:
        ...


class MySequentialSampler(MySampler[int]):
    r"""Samples elements sequentially, always in the same order.

    Args:
        data_source (Dataset): dataset to sample from
    """
    data_source: Sized

    def __init__(self, data_source: Sized) -> None:

The Source code contains the following remark
    # NOTE [ Lack of Default `__len__` in Python Abstract Base Classes ]
    #
    # Many times we have an abstract class representing a collection/iterable of
    # data, e.g., `torch.utils.data.Sampler`, with its subclasses optionally
    # implementing a `__len__` method. In such cases, we must make sure to not
    # provide a default implementation, because both straightforward default
    # implementations have their issues:
    #
    #   + `return NotImplemented`:
    #     Calling `len(subclass_instance)` raises:
    #       TypeError: 'NotImplementedType' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
    #
    #   + `raise NotImplementedError()`:
    #     This prevents triggering some fallback behavior. E.g., the built-in
    #     `list(X)` tries to call `len(X)` first, and executes a different code
    #     path if the method is not found or `NotImplemented` is returned, while
    #     raising an `NotImplementedError` will propagate and and make the call
    #     fail where it could have use `__iter__` to complete the call.
    #
    # Thus, the only two sensible things to do are
    #
    #   + **not** provide a default `__len__`.
    #
    #   + raise a `TypeError` instead, which is what Python uses when users call
    #     a method that is not defined on an object.
    #     (@ssnl verifies that this works on at least Python 3.7.)

The docs for the forward function give the dimensions of key, query and value as E_k, E_q, E_v respectively which is really confusing, since, if I am not mistaken they should all be the same.
The transformer paper, which is referenced in the docs, follows this convention, as far as I can tell.
Moreover, this seems to be implemented in torch.
we pass embed_dim to the functional implementation to check that it matches query_dim and check that key and value have the same shape.
We also comment the code, saying that the dimension of the query and key are expected to be the same, and, indeed, if they aren't the matrix multiplication will fail.
Proposed fix.
Replace E_k, E_q, E_v with E, E, E. We may also want to add explicit checking that all three are the same in a clearer way.
e.g.
assert query.shape[-1] == key.shape[-1], f"query has embedding dimension {query.shape[-1]} which does n't match key embedding dimension: {key.shape[-1]}"
assert key.shape == value.shape
I'd be happy to make the changes, if they would be approved!

indices : list[list[int]] is a list of list of indices

import torch

def test_it(N=1000, D=42, W=10):
    t = torch.randn(N, D)
    indices = [range(i, i + W) for i in range(0, N - W)]

    return None

It was mentioned in #68420 that max_unpool has troubles with dilation > 1 inputs.
The following example shows that the user could also run into the following issue:
To Reproduce
In [1]: import torch

In [2]: x = torch.rand(3, 10, 10, dtype=torch.double)

In [3]: x[:, 4, 4] = 10

In [4]: pool, idx = torch.nn.functional.max_pool2d(x, kernel_size=3, return_indices = True)
/home/nik/git/Quansight/pytorch/torch/nn/functional.py:735: UserWarning: Note that order of the arguments: ceil_mode and return_indices will changeto match the args list in nn.MaxPool2d in a future release.
  warnings.warn("Note that order of the arguments: ceil_mode and return_indices will change"

In [5]: unpool = torch.nn.functional.max_unpool2d(pool, idx, kernel_size=3)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

<ipython-input-5-c5cf8bc14f95> in <module>
----> 1 unpool = torch.nn.functional.max_unpool2d(pool, idx, kernel_size=3)

~/git/Quansight/pytorch/torch/nn/functional.py in max_unpool2d(input, indices, kernel_size, stride, padding, output_size)
    991     padding = _pair(padding)
    992     output_size = _unpool_output_size(input, kernel_size, _stride, padding, output_size)
--> 993     return torch._C._nn.max_unpool2d(input, indices, output_size)
    994

RuntimeError: Found an invalid max index: 85 (output volumes are of size 9x9

The problem here is that the output shape of max_pool is computed via floor operation, so we loose some information about the shape of an input to max_pool when we are trying to max_unpool back. 🚀 Feature
ParameterDict implements most, but not all methods from dict. In particular it doesn't have:
>>> set(dir({})) - set(dir(nn.ParameterDict()))
{'__class_getitem__',
 '__ior__',
 '__or__',
 '__reversed__',
 '__ror__',
 'copy',
 'fromkeys',
 'get',
 'popitem',
 'setdefault'}

Arguably copy, fromkeys and popitem are not particularly useful, as well as the various or methods.
However .get() and .setdefault() can make code much nicer.
Motivation
I'm implementing an optimizable optimizer with parameter specific moment and velocity.
The code looks something like this:
def __init__(self):
    self.cache = nn.ParameterDict()
    ...
def adjust(self, params):
    ...
    for name, param in params:
        m = self.cache.get('m', torch.zeros(param.shape))
        v = self.cache.get('v', torch.zeros(param.shape) + self.eps)
        ...

I can't define these parameter specific parameters in my __init__, since I only know the shape they need once the first optimization step has started.
Pitch
The documentation writes "ParameterDict is an ordered dictionary".
It seems that as such it should implement the standard python dictionary methods.
In fact, it already implements nearly all of them, so why not those last two?
Alternatives
I could write
if 'm' not in self.cache:
        self.cache[name]['m'] = torch.zeros(param.shape)
if 'v' not in self.cache 
        self.cache[name]['v'] = torch.zeros(param.shape) + self.eps
m = self.cache[name]['m']
v = self.cache[name]['v']

But it is 3 times as many lines of code, and any python developer would wonder "why doesn't this just use .get or .default?"

Composing release notes has historically been a very time consuming process. Until now, we would have one dedicated engineer from the PyTorch Core team manually categorize all the commits (usually about 3-3.5k commits)  every release, which is usually about a week's worth of full-time work.
In PyTorch 1.10, we made a significant improvement, by auto-categorizing about 30% (1k) of the 3.5k commits using this script that labeled PRs based on the files changed.

python3.6 test/test_cuda.py TestCuda.test_caching_pinned_memory_multi_gpu

🐛 Bug
storage_offset in _make_wrapper_subclass doesn't work.
To Reproduce
import torch

class WrapperTensor(torch.Tensor):
    elem: torch.Tensor

    __slots__ = ['elem']

    @staticmethod
    def __new__(cls, elem, *args, **kwargs):
        r = torch.Tensor._make_wrapper_subclass(  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
            cls, elem.size(),
            dtype=elem.dtype, layout=elem.layout,
            device=elem.device, requires_grad=elem.requires_grad,
            strides=elem.stride(), storage_offset=elem.storage_offset())
        r.elem = elem
        return r

    @classmethod
    def __torch_dispatch__(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        pass

x = torch.randn(2, 2)[:, 1]
print(x.storage_offset())                # prints 1
print(WrapperTensor(x).storage_offset()) # prints 0

Expected behavior
The WrapperTensor should report storage offset as 1.
cc @albanD @bdhirsh

Following some discussion about time to signal (TTS), ASAN tests are some of the longest CI jobs in PyTorch. Thus, to cut down overall time-to-signal for any pull request, we should focus on cutting down our ASAN test time.
One way to do this is to further shard the ASAN tests. This can be done by changing the num_test_shards variable here https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/.github/scripts/generate_ci_workflows.py#L417.
Currently, the asan tests are split into two jobs and they each take around 2hr4min each. You can try experimenting with 3 shards or 4 shards and document any time improvements.
One thing to note is that there is currently no "smart" sharding enabled for ASAN as I ran into trouble enabling it, so it will distribute the tests round robin style. If you'd like to try enabling the "smart" sharding based on previous test stats, you can try adding this line to the bottom of https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/.jenkins/pytorch/build-asan.sh.
  # export test times so that potential sharded tests that'll branch off this build will use consistent data
  python test/run_test.py --export-past-test-times

cc @seemethere @malfet @pytorch/pytorch-dev-infra
nodes.title: CI: Further shard ASAN tests
